request_payload.input: We are comparing two English natural-language-inference classifiers. We want to know which one better tracks who did what to whom when deciding whether a hypothesis follows from a premise, including cases where the two sentences use almost the same words. Recommend a public evaluation resource and scoring plan, and state what conclusion it would justify.
request_payload.instructions: Answer the research question from existing knowledge. Aim for 180–240 words and do not exceed 300 words. Do not browse or use external tools. Do not ask a follow-up question.

output_text: Use the ANLI-1 development set as the public evaluation resource, because its human-written hypotheses are designed to defeat models that rely on word overlap, and it contains many premise–hypothesis pairs with nearly identical lexical items but different entailment labels. From it, build a role-controlled subset: extract transitive clauses and keep pairs where the same content words occur but subject/object roles are reversed or altered, for example, “The dog bit the man” versus “The man bit the dog,” or “A woman is eating a cake” versus “A cake is eating a woman.” Use dependency parsing to tag agent and patient, and include only pairs with at least 80% content-word overlap. Score each classifier with: (1) overall three-way accuracy on the subset; (2) macro-F1 for entailment, neutral, and contradiction; (3) role-reversal accuracy, measuring correct labels when agent/patient swap; and (4) overlap-bias rate, the increase in entailment predictions as lexical overlap rises. Use paired bootstrap confidence intervals over sentence pairs. If one classifier has significantly higher role-reversal accuracy and lower overlap-bias while maintaining overall NLI accuracy, conclude that it better tracks who did what to whom rather than merely matching surface words.
